## Similar Courses {.unnumbered #similar-courses}

Other universities teach courses much like this one,
and many post their materials at no cost.
They are a good place to see a topic explained a second way.

Discrete mathematics and proofs:

- MIT's [6.042J *Mathematics for Computer Science*](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-spring-2015/)
  (Spring 2015, on MIT OpenCourseWare),
  with recorded lectures, readings and problem sets.
- Stanford's [CS 103 *Mathematical Foundations of Computing*](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs103/),
  with lecture slides and problem sets.
- The University of Washington's [CSE 311 *Foundations of Computing I*](https://courses.cs.washington.edu/courses/cse311/),
  with lecture slides and homework from past quarters.

Functional programming:

- Stanford's [CS 107 *Programming Paradigms*](https://see.stanford.edu/Course/CS107)
  (Spring 2008, on Stanford Engineering Everywhere),
  whose recorded lectures 19 to 23 and handouts introduce Scheme, Racket's parent language.
- Stanford's [CS 242 *Programming Languages*](https://stanford-cs242.github.io/f19/) (Fall 2019),
  with lecture notes on the lambda calculus and functional programming.
- Stanford's [CS 99 *Functional Programming and Theorem Proving in Lean 4*](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs99/),
  which carries functional programming over to writing proofs.

## Materials {.unnumbered}

I will distribute worksheets, homework, and lab materials on Canvas.
The lecture notes are on the [course notes site](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mcs/), listed in its menu bar.
Each chapter is also available as slides and as a PDF handout,
linked under **Other Formats** on the chapter's page.
